Background and Policy Description\nThis section\xa0provides background information and describes the context in which \nthe national monitoring program studied in this paper was introduced. In Section\xa0IA, \nwe describe the environmental policies in place in China during this period and \ndiscuss the local leaders’ role in achieving them. After that, the infrastructure put in \nplace to monitor these policies’ implementation is described in Section\xa0IB. Section\xa0IC \ndiscusses how the information presented in this section\xa0guides our analysis.\nA. Environmental Policies in China\nWhile the Chinese government’s priority during the past decades has largely been \nto stimulate economic growth, attention has lately shifted toward environmental pol-\nicies (Zheng and\xa0Kahn 2017).5 Starting in 2013, the National Air Quality Action \nPlan was set up to improve air quality by the end of 2017. As a part of China’s \nsuccessful “war on pollution” (Greenstone and\xa0Schwarz 2018), the plan laid out \nthe general ambition for the whole country and set differentiated goals for each \nregion. In January 2014, the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP) entered \ninto “contracts” with all 31 provinces and set up a  three-year air quality plan to \ndecrease the concentration of particulate matter (PM) in the whole country. In each \n“contract,” an air quality target for 2017 was set—resulting in different percentage \nreduction targets of   PM 2.5  / PM 10    for each province relative to the 2012 level.6\nThese centrally set targets are implemented by local government officials, who \nare incentivized to fulfill them through  performance-based promotions. Promotions \nare the key instrument used in China to ensure that local officials carry out pol-\nicies in line with the goals set by the central government (see Zheng and\xa0 Kahn \n2013, 2017, for further discussion of this topic). For a long time, the central gov-\nernment focused on economic performance and emphasized economic growth as \nthe key evaluation criteria for local officials’ promotion (Chen, Li, and\xa0Lu 2018). \nHowever, from the Twelfth  Five-Year Plan onward, the central government has used \nthe fulfilment of environmental performance targets as a requirement for the promo-\ntion of local  mayors (Zheng and\xa0Kahn 2013).\n5 The concentration of air pollutants in China is among the world’s highest and is a problem with serious health \nconsequences. Average   PM 2.5    (particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less) concentrations in \n2013 were 91 micrograms per cubic meter ( μg/ m   3  ), which is nine times the amount the World Health Organization \nconsiders safe. Estimates by Greenstone and\xa0Schwarz (2018) suggest that if these levels of pollution are sustained, \nit will result in a 6.5 year decline in life expectancy for the average resident.\n6 For the list of targets by province, see Table\xa0C3 in online Appendix\xa0C.VOL. 16 NO. 1 219\nAXBARD AND DENG: INFORMED ENFORCEMENT\nB. National Monitoring System\nTo address issues raised about limited coverage and quality of existing pollution \ndata, the central government introduced a new monitoring system as a part of its \n2013 National Air Quality Action Plan. This new system expanded coverage to all \nof China—introducing monitors in  prefecture-level cities that previously had no \nsystematic air pollution monitoring in place. In addition, cities with existing moni-\ntors received new updated monitors that could capture the wider range of pollutants \nincluded in the revised air pollution standards (notably,   PM 2.5   , widely regarded as \nthe key measure of ambient air pollution, was included for the first time). One of \nthe key features of the new system is that all monitoring stations report six pollut-\nants (  SO 2   ,   NO 2   , CO,   PM 10   ,   PM 2.5   , and   O 3   ) to the central government in real time \n(Greenstone et\xa0al. 2022). Hourly pollution data are then automatically published \nonline by the central government.\nThe new monitors were installed in three separate phases. The first phase was \nconducted in 2013 and focused on 74 major cities that represented the country’s \nkey population and economic centers.7 As part of the National Air Quality Action \nPlan, these cities were simultaneously targeted by a number of additional policies \naimed at reducing air pollution (MEP 2013).8 The second phase was implemented \nin 2014 for the 87 designated “environmental role model cities,” which face stricter \nand more frequent evaluation of environmental performance (MEP 2011; Brehm \nand\xa0Svensson 2020). The primary aim of the first two phases was to automate old \nmanual monitors, since 70\xa0percent of these cities already had pollution monitoring \nin place. The main expansion phase, which is the one we focus on in this paper, \nwas carried out in the following year when all 177 remaining  prefecture-level cities \n(53\xa0percent of all  prefecture-level divisions in China) received monitoring for the \nfirst time. After this final expansion, all  prefecture-level cities had at least one air \nquality monitor. These monitors all started transmitting information to the central \ngovernment on January\xa01, 2015.\nThe funding for the monitors was provided by the  province-level environmental \nbureaus. Once all equipment had been put in place, the  city-level environmental \nbureau was made responsible for the maintenance and operation of all monitors \nwithin the city. The local governments, which have incentives to report low levels \nof pollution because of the performance targets they face, could potentially do this \nby manipulating the recordings from the monitors. Such manipulation was facili-\ntated by the direct control of the monitors that the local governments were given. \nIndeed, several media sources have reported that such manipulation did occur (e.g., \nby spraying the monitor with water to reduce the recordings).9\n7 The Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei metropolitan region, the Yangtze River Delta, the Pearl River Delta, directly \nadministered municipalities, and provincial capitals.\n8 This included, e.g., stricter pollution reduction targets by 2017, prohibiting the construction of new  coal-fired \npower stations from 2015, different motor gasoline standards from 2013, reduced reliance on coal and increased \nconstruction of natural gas infrastructure, setting up regional environmental impact assessment and joint law \nenforcement, etc.\n9 See https://p.dw.com/p/32jqR and http://www.xinhuanet.com/politics/2018-08/09/c_1123244676.htm, for \ntwo examples.220 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\nRealizing that the data provided by local environmental protection bureaus might \nnot be reliable, the MEP decided to contract the operation of the monitor stations \nto private companies through a procurement process. According to official docu-\nments from the MEP, all of the monitors were operated by private companies on \nNovember\xa01, 2016. Monitors were procured through 12 contracts. Each contract \nwas designed to involve monitors in different provinces spread out over the country, \nto make it difficult for firms to select a given area. Six companies were selected, and \neach of them won two contracts. These firms were then paid directly by the MEP to \noperate the monitors.\nIn addition to the regular monitors in the  built-up area of each city, half of the \ncities were also assigned one background monitor. There are two main differences \nbetween the background monitors and the regular monitors: background monitors \nare installed outside of the  built-up area of the city and are usually placed in a local \nscenic area; more importantly, the readings from the background monitors are not \nused in the performance evaluation of local officials. Due to the different nature of \nthe background monitors, we are not including them in the main analysis.10\nC. Conceptual Framework and Sample Selection\nAs discussed in the previous section, the central government regulates (e.g., sets \npollution standards), while the local government is responsible for enforcing these \nregulations (e.g., by issuing fines to firms’ violating existing regulations). Our inter -\nest is in understanding to what extent the introduction of monitors helps the central \ngovernment hold the local government accountable for their actions and how that \naffects enforcement behavior and pollution at the local level. To capture this effect \nwe focus on the 177 cities that face the same regulations and receive monitoring \nfor the first time.11 Online Appendix Figure\xa0 D1 illustrates how the introduction \nof monitors changes access to information on pollution both within and between \ncities. Within cities, monitor readings will be mostly affected by firms located close \nto and upwind from a monitor.12 Between cities, information on a larger share of \n high-pollution activity will be available for those cities that installed a greater num-\nber of monitors (as shown in Figure\xa03).\nHence, the monitoring program that we study changes the capacity of the cen-\ntral government to collect information about pollution. This capacity changes both \n10 Including them in the analysis does not alter any of our results. This type of targeting is common practice in China (Wang and\xa0Yang 2022). Wang \nand\xa0Yang (2022) emphasize that focusing on areas where policies are initially implemented risks leading to biased \nestimates of policy impact because of the way these areas are selected and the incentives faced by leaders exposed \nto early policy experimentation.\n12 There is no exact cutoff for how far away from the monitor pollution could be picked up. In addition to \nthe change in monitoring capacity in 2015, the reassignment of monitors from the \nlocal government to external third parties in 2016 changes the information provision \nprocess and decouples the responsibility of providing information with the respon-\nsibility to enforce regulations. The intention of the central government is that this \nshift should improve data quality and reduce the scope for manipulation. Because \nthird parties are paid directly by the MEP, their incentives are arguably more aligned \nwith those of the central rather than the local government. In our analysis we will \nmainly focus on the overall effect of the monitors. However, in Section\xa0IVB we will \nshed some light on the potential importance of who is responsible for information \nprovision.\nII. Data\nIn this article, we combine several data sources that provide comprehensive \ninformation on the enforcement of environmental regulation and air pollution per -\nformance in cities that introduced air pollution monitors in 2015 (MEP 2014). \nSection\xa0IIA describes the new data on local air pollution enforcement that we col-\nlect and digitize. After that, Section\xa0IIB describes the two sets of data that we use to \nmeasure air pollution: a  satellite-based measure of the AOD and data from the mon-\nitoring stations. Enforcement Records and Firm Data\nTo fully understand the impact of new air quality monitors on enforcement activ-\nities and the consequences of those activities, we face some  data-related empirical \nchallenges: first, the need to measure the quantity (and the quality) of governments’ \nenforcement activities and, second, the need to link enforcement activities to the \nlocation of air quality monitors. We address these challenges by constructing a new \ndataset on local enforcement of air pollution regulation in China using records col-\nlected from local environmental bureaus by the Institute of Public and Environmental \nAffairs (IPE) (IPE 2017). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt \nto fully track enforcement activities carried out by local environmental bureaus in \nChina. To identify where these enforcement activities occur, we  georeference all \nmajor manufacturing firms in China using the Annual Survey of Industrial Firms \n(ASIF) (National Bureau of Statistics 2013) and link these to the IPE records.\nEnforcement Records.—We collected all 55,184 enforcement records carried out \nfrom 2010 to 2017 in the 177  prefecture-level cities in our sample. Figure\xa0A1 in \nonline Appendix\xa0A provides an example of what these records look like and the type \nof information they contain. Each record includes details about the violating firm, \na description of the violation, a reference to the regulation that has been violated, \nand the local environmental bureau’s enforcement action. Using a classification 222 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\nalgorithm described in detail in online Appendix\xa0A.1, we categorize enforcement \nrecords in two dimensions. First, we identify what type of violation has been logged \nand whether this relates to air pollution, water pollution, waste pollution, or proce-\ndural violations. In total, we classify 24,691 records as being related to violations \nof air pollution regulations. Second, we identify what type of action has been taken \nby the local environmental bureau and in which quarter and year it was carried \nout. For 95\xa0percent of the enforcement records related to air pollution, the actions \nbelong to one or several of the following four categories: suspending production \n(52\xa0percent), ordering replacements/upgrading of the equipment (54\xa0percent), levy-\ning fines (48\xa0percent), or issuing a warning (15\xa0percent).\nFirm Data and  Georeferencing.—To be able to track where and against which \nfirms  local environmental bureaus choose to enforce regulations, we use data from \nthe 2013 ASIF. This survey is conducted by the National Bureau of Statistics. It \nincludes all  state-owned industrial enterprises and all private industrial enterprises \nwith annual sales exceeding ¥5 million. This corresponds to about 90 percent of \nall manufacturing firms in China and thus covers all major industrial polluters.13 \nPrevious versions of the ASIF data have been used in a number of papers (see, e.g., \nSong, Storesletten, and\xa0Zilibotti 2011; Brandt, Van Biesebroeck, and\xa0Zhang 2012; \nHuang et\xa0al. 2017). We focus on the 2013 version of the survey, which is the latest \navailable, and restrict our sample to firms that started operating before 2010 (the \nfirst year of our analysis). This allows us to gain an understanding of the underly-\ning distribution of manufacturing firms. Before linking the data to the enforcement \nrecords, we use detailed firm address information to identify the exact geographical \nlocation of all firms in the data. The process used for this  georeferencing is outlined \nin online Appendix\xa0A.1. Panel\xa0C in online Appendix Figure\xa0D2 shows the location \nof all the ASIF firms in our sample. Finally, we link our collection of enforcement \nrecords to the underlying distribution of manufacturing firms in the ASIF. Out of our \n55,184 records, 52 percent of them refer to enforcement actions against firms in the \nASIF data. Panel\xa0D in online Appendix Figure\xa0D2 shows the geographical distribu-\ntion of enforcement activities against these manufacturing firms.\nB. AOD measures \nthe degree to which aerosol particles prevent the transmission of light by absorption \nor scattering and can therefore be used as a measure of local pollution. Formally, \nAOD is defined as the negative of the natural logarithm of the fraction of radiation \n(e.g., light) that is not scattered or absorbed. We aggregate AOD at \ndifferent geographical levels—ranging from the pixel intersecting with the monitor \n(approximately 11 km × 11 km), to the city center around the monitors (10 to 50 \nkm from a monitor) and surrounding areas (beyond 50 km of a monitor). Main Sample and Summary Statistics\nTo supplement our analysis, we collect additional data on monthly weather con-\nditions (CMA 2017), quarterly dominant wind direction (CMA 2017), résumés of \nall mayors during our sample period (Jiang 2017), and city-level aggregates of citi-\nzens’ online searches for a set of keywords related to pollution (Baidu 2017). Online \nAppendix\xa0A.3 describes this additional data in detail and the procedure used for \ncollecting it. Using the data on pollution and enforcement described above together \nwith these additional sources, we construct three main samples for our analysis—all \ncovering the 177  prefecture-level cities that installed monitors in 2015. Summary \nstatistics for these three samples are presented in online Appendix Table\xa0C1.\nPanel\xa0A reports information for the  firm-level data. We rely on the 2013 ASIF \nand restrict the sample to firms that started operating before 2010 (the first year of \nour analysis) and that are located within 50 km of an air quality monitor.17 This \nleaves us with a total sample of 36,103 firms. The majority of these firms are pri-\nvate (81\xa0percent) and cover a wide range of different industries (online Appendix \nTable\xa0C5 reports the industry composition for our sample). On average, the firms \nin our sample are located 19 km from a monitor. However, as depicted in online \nAppendix Figure\xa0D9, the spatial distribution of firms is skewed, and 40\xa0percent of \nfirms are located within 10 km of a monitor. For a given firm in our sample, the \nprobability of receiving an air-pollution-related enforcement action in a quarter \nis 0.5\xa0percent. Such an enforcement action most commonly requests that the firm  \nupgrade their equipment, but suspension of operation and issuing fines are also com-\nmon. Violations relating to water pollution regulations or conducting a procedural \nviolation are of a comparable magnitude (0.29\xa0percent and 0.52\xa0percent, respec-\ntively). Most (more than 75\xa0percent) of the enforcement actions were taken after the \nintroduction of air quality monitors.\nPanel\xa0B reports the summary statistics for the  city-level data. For this sample we \nconsider pollution as well as enforcement at the aggregate city level.18 The cities \nwe study are small by Chinese standards and have an average population of around \n340,000. The average size of our sample (measured by both the urban population and \nthe size of  the built-up area) are one-third of the country average. However, the air \npollution level in our sample (measured by AOD) is only slightly lower (10\xa0percent) \nthan the country average.19 On average the cities in our sample have 2.8 monitors \ninstalled, and about 4.2 firms face an environmental enforcement action related to \nair pollution per quarter. Out of these 4.2 firms, 1.5 are ASIF firms. Impact of the Monitors\nThis section\xa0describes the impact of monitoring on local government enforcement \nactivities and pollution. We start by discussing what determines where monitors are \ninstalled in Section\xa0IIIA, since this is key for our empirical analysis. Then, we pres-\nent our  firm-level empirical strategy and the corresponding results in Section\xa0IIIB. \nIn Section\xa0IIIC, we move from studying the local effects of monitoring to the aggre-\ngate city effects—exploiting differences in the number of monitors installed.\nA. Assignment and Location of Monitors\nThe MEP provided detailed instructions for how many monitors that should be \ninstalled in each city and where they should be located. All the monitors were installed \nin the so-called “ built-up area”—the main urban center of the  prefecture-level city. \nThe number of monitors assigned to each city was determined by the city’s popu-\nlation size and the geographical size of the  built-up area. Cities are assigned to one \nof four groups (corresponding to the installation of one, two, four, or six monitors), \ndetermined by the criteria that assigns it to the highest group. The detailed assign-\nment criterion, which we use for identification in our  city-level analysis, is presented \nin online Appendix Table\xa0C2.\nThe location of these monitors is depicted in the map in panel\xa0 A of online \nAppendix Figure\xa0D2. While the exact parameters used by the central government \nfor deciding the precise geographic location of each monitor are unknown, official \ngovernment documents report that the location was chosen by a simulation method \nthat took surrounding buildings, traffic, and the direction of seasonal winds into \naccount to make sure that the monitors captured a fair representation of local pollu-\ntion. To shed light on what determines the placement decision, we investigate how \nthe location of monitors relates to the spatial distribution and trends in enforcement \nactivities and pollution.\nWe start by investigating the spatial distribution of enforcement activities and how \nthese change with the introduction of monitors. Figure\xa01, panel\xa0A shows a binned \nscatterplot of the probability that a firm has any enforcement record related to air pol-\nlution in a quarter by the distance to the closest monitor. Black dots indicate the mean \nprobability during the period before air quality monitors were introduced, and red dia-\nmonds show the mean probability in the  post-period. The graph shows that the average \nquarterly probability of a firm receiving any air-pollution-related enforcement action \nis around 0.0021 before 2015, and that this probability does not seem to depend on \nthe distance to the ( planned)  monitor ( i.e., there is no gradient in enforcement activity \nin the  pre-period) . This provides some first evidence suggesting that monitors are not \nendogenously placed in localities with differential levels of enforcement. Figure\xa01, \npanel\xa0B shows another binned scatterplot that instead plots the trends in enforcement 226 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\nfor our treatment and control firms (firms located within/ beyond 10 km of a monitor) . \nThe graph shows that both groups of firms face similar trends as well as levels of \nenforcement in the years before the monitors are installed.\nNext, we investigate the pollution level and trends (measured by AOD) in areas \nwhere monitors are eventually installed and compare it with surrounding areas. Due \nto the nature of the AOD data, we are not able to use as  fine-grained spatial infor -\nmation as in the above analysis, but instead compare the AOD in the pixel where the \nmonitor is located (which are approximately 11 km\xa0 ×\xa011 km) to the AOD in the city \ncenter beyond the monitor ( 10–50 km from a monitor) and the area surrounding the \ncity center (beyond 50 km of a monitor). The first two groups roughly correspond to \nthe treatment and control groups in Figure\xa01, panel\xa0B. Figure\xa01, panel\xa0C shows that \nthe pollution level in the pixels where the monitors are located is above average in \nboth the city center and surrounding area (suggesting that the central government’s \nalgorithm is successfully targeting  high-pollution areas). However, importantly \nthese areas were on a similar trend to both other areas within the city center as well Figure\xa01. Firm-Level Evidence\nFigure\xa01, panels\xa0A and\xa0B suggest that there was a significant increase in enforce-\nment activity against firms located close to a monitor once the monitors were \ninstalled in 2015. The results are consistent with extensive media reporting that local \nenvironmental bureaus step up environmental inspections close to the monitors. We \ndocument some of this evidence in Figure\xa0D10 in online Appendix\xa0D, which shows \na list of news articles generated from a search on the Chinese search engine Baidu \nusing the keywords “monitors,” “surrounding area,” and “check.” The list includes \na large number of articles discussing how local governments organize their environ-\nmental inspections around the monitors. Some examples 21 include cities that draw \nspecial zones around their air quality monitors and send teams of inspectors to those \nzones, to ensure that firms comply with national environmental regulations. Other \nsources mention that city governments hire volunteers from the public to inspect air \npollution from venues within a certain distance from the monitors. Finally, several \nsources 22 suggest that mayors take a special interest in these inspections by, for \nexample, directly appointing officials to this task or by visiting surrounding areas. \nThis further underlines the weight that mayors put on the recordings from the mon-\nitors because of the performance incentives that they face.\nFirm Level: Event Study.—To investigate the relationship between monitors and \nenforcement formally, we estimate a flexible nonparametric event study specifica-\ntion. If we denote a generic firm by  i , with  i ∈ j, p , where  j  denotes a  four-digit \nindustry,  p  a province, and  t  a generic quarter, our model can be written as\n(1)   y ijpt   =  δ i   +  θ jt   +  η pt   +     ∑ \nd=0–5 km  15–20 km\n     \nd≠20–50 km   \n       ∑ \nk=Q1/2010  Q4/2017\n     \nk≠Q4/2014   \n    β dk    m  i  dk  +  ϵ ijpt   ,\nwhere   y ijpt    is an indicator for enforcement;   δ i    is a firm fixed effect;   θ jt    and   η pt    rep-\nresent, respectively,  industry-by-time and  province-by-time fixed effects;   m  i  dk   is \nan indicator for any monitor being within  d  km of a firm in quarter  k ; and   ϵ ijpt    is \nthe error term. Because we condition on firm as well as on  industry-by-time and \n province-by-time fixed effects, parameter estimates capture the average (across \nindustries and provinces) effect of monitoring on the differential change in enforce-\nment across firms in the same industry or province. This specification addresses \ntwo important concerns. First, we ensure that we estimate the impact of monitor -\ning within the same  regulatory environment (pollution reduction targets vary across \n20 The pattern shown in Figure\xa01, panel\xa0C is confirmed by a formal test of the  pre-trends, which shows no sig-\nnificant differences between the three areas in the five years prior to monitor installment.\n21 www.163.com/dy/article/H4HC2IIH0534B975.html.\n22 newpaper.dahe.cn/dhb/html/2017-12/28/content_212745.htm.228 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\nprovinces as  discussed in Section\xa0I). Second, we allow for different enforcement \ntrends depending on local industrial composition at baseline. We use the quarter \nbefore the introduction of the monitors and firms 20–50 km from the monitor as \nreference categories and estimate   β dk    for  d ∈  {0–5 km, 5–10 km, 10–15 km, 15–20 \nkm}  . Equation\xa0 (1) allows us to estimate the temporal and spatial relationship \nbetween monitors and enforcement activity. Hence, it is informative about the key \nidentification assumption for our analysis (parallel trends in enforcement for firms \nlocated at different distances from the monitors) as well as the spatial reach of mon-\nitors. We cluster standard errors at the city level to account for correlation of errors \nacross firms and time within cities.23\nFigure\xa02 reports the results from estimating equation\xa0 (1). We present the estimates \nin four separate event study graphs, each showing how enforcement activity changes \naround the introduction of monitors for firms within 0–5 km, 5–10 km, 10–15 km, \nand 15–20 km of the monitors relative to firms 20–50 km from the monitors (the \nreference category). In all four graphs, there is no evidence of any differential trends \nleading up to the intervention—lending credibility to the main identification assump-\ntion of parallel trends. After the introduction of the monitors, we see a substantial \nincrease in enforcement activity close to the monitors. This  step-up in enforcement \nis particularly pronounced within 0–5 km of the monitors but is noticeable also for \nfirms 5–10 km from the monitors. For firms 15–20 km from the monitors, there is no \ndifferential change in enforcement activity during our sample period.24\nFirm Level: Main Results.—Guided by the results in the previous section, we use \na simplified  DiD specification to provide an estimate of the magnitude of the effect. \nThis specification compares firms within and beyond 10 km of a monitor, but our \nresults are robust to using 15 km or 20 km instead. Taken together, these results suggest that local \ngovernments respond to monitoring by shifting both the intensity and the strictness \nof enforcement toward high polluters.\nFirm Level: Responsiveness.—Next, we investigate whether monitors make local \ngovernments’ enforcement efforts more responsive to recorded pollution. The main \nempirical challenge inherent in studying this is the endogeneity of local pollution. \nTo overcome this challenge, we exploit two different sources of plausibly exogenous \nvariation: local rainfall shocks and wind direction.\nWe start by investigating rainfall shocks. First, we establish that local rainfall \nshocks are important determinants of local pollution. For each city, we construct \nan indicator (  Rain > x ̃     ) for whether the quarterly rainfall is above the median for that \ncity or not. Online Appendix Table\xa0C6 shows estimates of the relationship between \nthe average pollution recordings across the monitors in the city and this high rain-\nfall indicator, controlling for city and time fixed effects. Results show that aver -\nage pollution recordings are consistently about  7–9\xa0percent lower in quarters with \nabove-median rainfall. These effects are substantially stronger at higher levels of \npollution, which are arguably more important for local policy response, where, e.g., \nthe share of days that have any reading classified as heavily polluted ( AQI > 200 ) \nis reduced by 22\xa0percent (0.024/0.11). We then explore how enforcement activities \nrespond to pollution monitoring in the presence of rainfall shocks by estimating an \naugmented version of our baseline model (equation\xa0 (2)) that introduces interactions \nwith the quarterly rainfall shock.26\nThe results from this analysis are reported in panel\xa0A of Table\xa02. Column\xa01 adds \nthe rainfall shock and its interaction with our main treatment variable (  m  it  10 km  ). \nTwo main takeaways emerge. First, enforcement activities do not respond to rain-\nfall shocks in the absence of monitors—suggesting that there is no direct effect \nof rainfall on enforcement. Second, the effect of monitors on enforcement is sub-\nstantially smaller (0.0043 − 0.0018 = 0.0025) when rainfall levels are above the \nmedian (i.e., when pollution levels are lower) as opposed to when rainfall levels are \nbelow the median (0.0043) (i.e., when pollution levels are higher). These results \nsuggest that the information captured by the monitors is important for the enforce-\nment actions taken by the local governments and that the monitors make the local \ngovernment responsive to changes in local pollution. To investigate whether this result \nreflect a general increase in the enforcement responsiveness in times of high pollu-\ntion (as opposed to simply a stronger willingness to reduce the monitors’ pollution \nrecordings) , we estimate a model with the full set of interactions. Column\xa02 reports \nthe results from estimating this model and shows suggestive evidence ( significant at \nthe 10\xa0percent level)  that, in the presence of monitoring, there is a general increase \nin enforcement during periods of high pollution also in areas farther away from the \n26 We prefer taking this reduced-form approach instead of instrumenting local pollution levels since we only \nhave pollution data from the monitors from 2015  onward.232 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\nmonitor. In this section, we will discuss and investigate two threats to \nthis interpretation of our results.\nThe first concern we will address is the risk that our results are affected by \n time-specific policies or shocks that  coincide with the introduction of monitors. \nThis could be the case if firms close to a monitor respond differently to such a \nshock compared to firms farther away. For this to bias our results, firms within the \nsame industry/province would need to be differently affected depending on their \ndistance to a monitor (since our baseline specification controls for both  four-digit \n industry-by-time and  province-by-time fixed effects). While we are not aware of \nany such policies or shocks, we investigate this potential concern further by con-\nducting three additional tests. First, we use equation\xa0 (2) to look at environmental \nenforcement that is not related to air pollution. The results are reported in panel\xa0A of \nTable\xa0C7 in the online Appendix. For enforcement related to water pollution, solid \nwaste pollution, and procedure violation, estimates are small and statistically insig-\nnificant. Second, panel\xa0B of online Appendix Table\xa0C7 gradually includes controls \nthat interact baseline characteristics with time fixed effects to our main specification. \nFirst we address the fact that our sample period overlaps with the relocation of basic \nmanufacturing away from coastal regions stipulated in the Twelfth  Five-Year Plan. \nColumn\xa02 addresses this issue by including the distance from the city to the coast \ninteracted with time fixed effects. Then we address the fact that policies or shock \nexposure might be related to firm characteristics in column\xa03 and interact the num-\nber of employees and ownership status with time fixed effects. Finally, we control \nfor city-by-time fixed effects in column\xa04. Estimates remain of a comparable magni-\ntude and are highly statistically significant across all specifications. Third, we con-\nduct placebo tests in which we estimate the specification used to produce Figure\xa02, \nbut instead of the distance to the closest monitor, we use the distance to the local \nenvironmental bureau or the distance to the city’s firm centroid. We do this to inves-\ntigate whether there is a differential response in enforcement after 2015 depending \non plausible spatial determinants related to both the costs and returns from enforce-\nment.27 Figure\xa0D5 of online Appendix\xa0D shows that there are no detectable changes \nin the gradients of enforcement activity pre- and post-2015. To further validate our \nmain results, we include the distances to both the environmental bureau and the firm \ncentroid in our main specification and interact the distance bins with the time fixed \neffects. Due to the high correlation between monitor location and these measures, \nour results are slightly less precise, but largely unaffected when including this full \n27 We argue that the costs of enforcement are likely to be lower close to the environmental bureau (where moni-\ntors are often placed) and that the returns from enforcement are likely greater in central areas (due to a greater con-\ncentration of population and economic activity). To calculate firm centroids for each city, we use the geographical \ndistribution of all ASIF firms. The firm centroid is a single point representing the barycenter of all firms.234 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\nset of controls.28 Taken together, these results suggest that the  step-up in enforce-\nment behavior that we observe is indeed driven by the monitors.\nThe second concern we will investigate is whether the results we observe above \nare affected by spillovers. This could be the case if our control group (firms farther \naway from the monitor) is also affected by the introduction of monitors, e.g., if firms \nobserve and respond to enforcement actions against neighbors, or if the local gov-\nernment reduces enforcement efforts against firms far from a monitor. Depending \non the nature of the spillovers, these could lead us to either over- or underestimate \nthe impact of monitoring. Our first attempt to address this issue is to reexamine the \npatterns in the raw data presented in Figure\xa01,\xa0panels\xa0A and\xa0B. The figures show that \nbefore 2015, enforcement levels and trends are the same in both treated and control \nfirms. After 2015, there is a clear  step-up of enforcement against firms within 10 \nkm of a monitor, while firms farther away continue on a similar  upward-sloping \nenforcement trend. If these firms would have been affected by spillovers, we would \nhave expected a change in their enforcement trend post-2015. While these patterns \nin the raw data are reassuring, they do not necessarily rule out spillovers, since we \ndo not know the counterfactual trends. Therefore, we move on to conduct an anal-\nysis at the  city level in the following section\xa0where we analyze aggregate outcomes \nthat take any within city spillovers into account. In addition, we specifically inves-\ntigate the impact of the intensity of monitoring on  nonmonitored areas following an \napproach similar in spirit to the work by Crépon et\xa0al. (2013).\nC.  City-Level Evidence\nTo study the impact of monitoring at the  city level, we exploit variation in the \nintensity of the monitoring program. This approach allows us to infer the overall \nimpact of more extensive monitoring on both enforcement and pollution. To con-\nduct this analysis, we exploit the criteria set up by the central government when \nimplementing the monitoring program ( listed in Table\xa0C2 in online Appendix\xa0C) \nand compare outcomes in cities that installed different numbers of monitors. The \nargument behind this approach is that a larger number of monitors will ensure that \nofficials are held accountable for a greater share of the overall pollution in a city. \nFigure\xa03 illustrates this point for our data by showing how the number of monitors \nassigned to a city is related to the share of  high-pollution activity that is covered \nby a monitor. We again rely on the ESR database to identify  high-polluting firms. \nTo adjust for firm size, our baseline measure of  high-pollution activity covered \ncalculates the share of a city’s  high-polluting firms’ revenue that fall within 10 km \nof a monitor.29 The figure shows that the share of  high-pollution activity covered \nwithin 10 km of a monitor increases monotonically with the number of monitors, \nfrom 20\xa0percent for cities with 1 monitor to more than 80\xa0percent for cities with 6 \n28 The main estimate in column\xa01 of panel\xa0A in Table\xa01 changes from 0.0033 to 0.0017 and is significant at the \n5\xa0percent level.\n29 The ESR database allows us to identify high/low-polluting firms (i.e., whether the firm is on the list or not). \nWe use the revenue share to scale our measure by firm size and thereby get closer to the share of overall pollution \nthat is covered by the monitors. We report marginal effects in online Appendix Table\xa0C8. Our baseline \nestimate suggests that an additional monitor increases coverage by 11\xa0percentage \npoint (a 30\xa0percent increase compared to the mean) . Again, we document the robustness \nof these results with respect to the sample studied and the firms considered and sep-\narate by cutoff in online Appendix Tables\xa0C10, C11, C13.\nCity Level: Spillovers.—We now turn to separate the aggregate  city-level \neffect of monitoring into direct and spillover effects. To perform this analysis \nwe exploit the same four identification strategies as above but calculate the out-\ncomes separately for the monitoring station ( within 10 km) , the city center (  10–\n50 km from a monitor) , and the surrounding areas ( beyond 50 km) . This allows \nus to observe how enforcement behavior and pollution change in monitored as \nwell as in  nonmonitored areas. Observing this is important since officials could \npotentially reallocate enforcement effort from  nonmonitored to monitored areas \nin response to the policy. If such behavior took place, we would expect to see a \nreduction in enforcement activity in  the nonmonitored areas of cities that installed \na greater number of monitors compared to cities that installed fewer monitors. Our \napproach is similar in spirit to the work by Crépon et\xa0al. ( 2013) , which identifies \nspillovers by investigating the response of  nontreated firms in regions with differ -\nent treatment saturation.\nOnline Appendix Table\xa0C14 reports these results and shows that while we see \nthat a greater number of monitors led to a substantial increase in enforcement close \nto the monitors, estimates for the city center and surrounding areas are still pos-\nitive, though smaller and not significantly different from zero for most empirical \nstrategies. This suggests that the increase in enforcement close to the monitors that \nwe observe in the firm-level analysis is not driven by a reallocation of enforcement \neffort from  nonmonitored areas. Estimates for pollution show reductions across the \ncity. While DiD and IV estimates are comparable across areas, discontinuity esti-\nmates suggest smaller pollution reductions in surrounding areas (with point esti-\nmates ranging from from 49\xa0percent to 78\xa0percent of the size of the estimates for the \narea close to the monitor). These estimates suggest that there are positive spillovers \n(reduction in pollution) in areas not covered by a monitor. There are a number of \npotential explanations consistent with these results. One possibility is that there is a \nreduction in the spread of pollution from the  high-pollution areas close to the mon-\nitors, where we document an increase in enforcement, to the  nonmonitored areas \nof the city. An alternative explanation is that the step-up in enforcement in the city \ncenter has deterrence effects affecting the pollution behavior of  noncovered firms as \nwell. However, we are careful in not interpreting these estimates too strongly since \nsatellite-based measures of pollution are highly spatially correlated. Hence, these VOL. 16 NO. 1 243\nAXBARD AND DENG: INFORMED ENFORCEMENT\neffects could partly reflect the inability of satellites to pick up differences in pollu-\ntion at a high spatial resolution.\nTo sum up, the results in this section\xa0show that an increase in monitoring intensity \n(i.e., a greater coverage of  high polluters in a city) leads to enforcement against a \nlarger number of firms (in particular those close to a monitor) and an overall reduc-\ntion in AOD in the entire city. Point estimates are consistent across four different \nempirical strategies but vary in how precise they are. The RD approach has the key \nadvantage of requiring weaker assumptions for causal inference, but the power of \nthis analysis is lower, and it rests on a limited sample close to the threshold. We \ntherefore focus on the DiD specification, which produces the most conservative and \nprecise estimates, in the following mechanism section.\nIV . Mechanisms\nIn this section, we investigate the potential channels through which the informa-\ntion captured by the monitors strengthens enforcement and reduces pollution. In \nSection\xa0 IV A, we explore whether monitors improve  top-down and/or  bottom-up \naccountability. Thereafter, we document in Section\xa0IVB how a change in the infor -\nmation provision process that separates the responsibility to provide information \nfrom the responsibility to enforce regulations affects our results.\nA.  Top-Down Accountability: Performance Incentives\nAs discussed in Section\xa0IA, pollution reduction is one of the criteria that local \nleaders are evaluated on, and their performance determines their probability of pro-\nmotion. Hence, a natural interpretation of our main findings is that monitors improve \nthe central government’s ability to evaluate how well local officials perform. In this \nsection, we investigate this proposed mechanism more directly by exploiting het-\nerogeneity in the promotion incentives faced by local officials. To get a plausibly \nexogenous measure of local promotion incentives, we use two unique features of the \nChinese political system. First, we use the timing of the National People’s Congress \n(NPC), which is held every five years and determines when political promotions are \nmade in China. As documented in Xi, Yao, and\xa0Zhang (2018), the average proba-\nbility of promotion for a city official in the last year of a political cycle (when the \nNPC is held) is nearly three times that of the first year in a cycle. We then combine \nthis information with two official requirements for mayors of  prefecture-level cities: \nthat they retire at age 60 and serve for at least three years in a post. This means that \ncity officials above the age of 57 at the time of the NPC face a discontinuously lower \nprobability of being promoted and, therefore, weaker performance incentives (as \ndocumented in Xi, Yao, and\xa0Zhang 2018).\nTo conduct this analysis, we collect data on the main mayor in office in the \nyear when the monitors were introduced and calculate their age at the thirteenth \nNPC, which was held in March 2018. If the information provided by the monitors \nstrengthens the ability of the central government to hold local officials account-\nable, we would expect smaller effects of monitoring for cities with mayors who \nwere above 57 years of age at the time of the congress. Mayors who are not facing 244 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024\n promotion incentives are arguably less likely to work to achieve stricter enforcement \nof regulations.\nTo test our hypothesis about promotion incentives formally, we add an interaction \nterm between the number of monitors in a city and the age of the mayor at the time \nof the congress to equation\xa0 (4). As mayors’ work experience might confound our \nanalysis, we use a similar idea to the RD design and plot the differential effects (i.e., \nthe interaction terms) of an additional monitor on both pollution and enforcement \nby the age of the mayor at the time of the congress in Figure\xa06. We set the baseline \nto the mayor who is 58 years old at the time of the congress and estimate other coef-\nficients relative to this. A distinctive feature of both graphs is that the effects are not \ndistinguishable from the baseline if the mayor is older than 58. At age 57, we see a \nsubstantial jump of the estimates in both graphs. The fact that estimates jump at 57 \nand are then consistent for lower ages suggests that our results are indeed driven by \nperformance incentives and not by work experience or other  age-related character -\nistics (for which we would not expect a jump at age 57). To further ensure that this \nresult is not driven by confounding factors, we perform a corresponding analysis of \ncity baseline characteristics in Figure\xa0D11 in the online Appendix. This balance test \nshows that the number of monitors, the size of the city, and economic activity as \nproxied by lights at night, as well as baseline pollution and enforcement activity, are \nsmooth around the 57 age threshold—suggesting that our results are driven by the \ndifference in promotion incentives.\nWe report the regression results of a simplified version of the results presented \nin Figure\xa0 6 in Table\xa0 C15 in online Appendix\xa0 C, where we instead interact the \nnumber of monitors with whether a mayor is below the age cutoff at the time of \nthe NPC. Panel\xa0A displays the results for air pollution, and panel\xa0B displays the \nresults on enforcement. In the first column, we use the full sample from our main \nanalysis in Section\xa0IIIC, and we then subsequently restrict the sample to mayors \ncloser to the performance age cutoff ( again following the RD logic) . The coeffi-\ncients for the number of monitors now correspond to the effect for the mayors with \nweaker performance incentives, while the interaction term shows the additional \neffect of monitors in the presence of promotion incentives. These terms are all \nstatistically significant and suggest that the performance incentive increases the \nresponse by between  65 and 87\xa0percent. A corresponding balance table is reported \nin online Appendix Table\xa0C16. This shows that while there are some imbalances \nwhen we compare all cities with mayors above the threshold with all cities with \nmayors below the threshold, these differences are substantially smaller and no \nlonger statistically significant when we move close to the threshold. We conclude \nfrom this analysis that a  preexisting incentive scheme similar to those that are \ntypically proposed to address the principal–agent problem is key in order for mon-\nitoring to be effective.\nSince the information from the monitors is also provided to the public online, an \nalternative explanation for our main results is that monitors strengthen  bottom-up \naccountability. To investigate whether this is a plausible driver of our results, we \nestimate the impact of the number of monitors on online search behavior using \nequation\xa0 (4). We report results in online Appendix Table\xa0C17, which shows that \nwhile the point estimate on all five keywords is positive, the estimates are small, and VOL. 16 NO. 1 245\nAXBARD AND DENG: INFORMED ENFORCEMENT\nnone of them are significantly different from zero. Hence, we do not find any evi-\ndence suggesting that the number of monitors improves information acquisition by \nthe local population. This test compares cities with more or less comprehensive \nmonitoring and not cities with and without monitoring. The result therefore does \nnot rule out that citizens with access to monitors may exert more pressure on local \nleaders than citizens without access to any monitoring. However, the impact of more \ncomprehensive monitoring on enforcement and pollution that we document does not \nseem to be driven by increased dissemination of information to the public.\nB. Changing Information Provision\nAlthough providing incentives for performance is a common approach to deal \nwith the principal–agent problem, it has long been recognized that  high-powered \nincentives can also distort the type of effort exerted or even encourage various harm-\nful activities focused on improving indicators of performance (Figlio and\xa0Winicki \n2005; Banerjee, Duflo, and\xa0Glennerster 2008; Fisman and\xa0Wang 2017; Acemoglu \net\xa0 al. 2020). Manipulating data on which performance is evaluated is one strat-\negy that has been documented in a series of studies (Jacob and\xa0Levitt 2003; Figlio \nand\xa0Getzler 2006; Banerjee, Duflo, and\xa0Glennerster 2008; Sandefur and\xa0Glassman \n2015; Greenstone et\xa0al. 2022). In this section, we study whether the structure of the \ninformation provision system could mitigate such concerns. In particular, our inter -\nest lies in understanding whether a separation of the agent responsible for providing \ninformation from the agent responsible for enforcing regulations affects the qual-\nity of information, and whether such quality improvements can, in turn, strengthen \naccountability and government performance (i.e., change behavior of the enforcing \nagent).Figure\xa06. Discussion and Concluding Remarks\nThis study uses the introduction of a pollution monitoring program in China to \ninvestigate the impact on local government enforcement of environmental regula-\ntions. Exploiting  georeferenced firm data matched with enforcement records, we \nfind that enforcement is stepped up against firms located within 10 km of a moni-\ntor. This resulted in an increase in enforcement in highly polluted areas in the city, \nwhich is where the monitors were placed. We further document that monitoring \naffects enforcement by altering which firms are targeted by local governments and \nby strengthening the responsiveness to local pollution shocks.\nTo study the aggregate impact of the policy, we conduct a  city-level analysis and \ncompare enforcement and pollution levels in cities that installed different numbers \nof monitors and thus introduced differential coverage of local pollution activity. Our \nbaseline analysis shows that one additional monitor (a 30\xa0percent increase in cov-\nerage of  high-pollution activity) leads to about a 15\xa0percent increase in the number \nof firms that face regulatory enforcement and a subsequent 3\xa0percent reduction in \n city-level pollution. The increase in enforcement is focused on the areas close to the \nmonitor, while pollution is reduced across the city. Given that the policy assigned \na median of three monitors per city, this corresponds to a substantial reduction in \noverall pollution. Our estimates suggest a 0.42–0.86  μg/ m   3   reduction in average   \nPM 2.5    per additional monitor.40 Previous literature suggests that such a decrease in \npollution could have significant health and economic benefits, which would likely \nexceed the cost of the program in the short run.41\nAn examination of possible mechanisms suggests that the monitoring program is \neffective because it enables the central government to hold local government offi-\ncials accountable for their actions. We support this claim by showing that monitoring \nis substantially more effective in localities where local officials face performance \nincentives. Finally, we document suggestive evidence showing that monitors deliver \nmore reliable information when local governments are not involved in information \nreporting and are solely responsible for enforcement. When such an information \n40 We arrive at the estimate of 0.42 (0.86)  μg/ m   3  , the lower (upper) bound, as follows. (2020), e.g., document that \na permanent decrease of 10  μg/ m   3   in China leads to annual savings of more than $10 billion in health spending. \nAnother cost of heavy air pollution in developing countries is the loss of productivity—Chang et\xa0al. (2016) and He, \nLiu, and\xa0Salvo (2019) find that a 10  μg/ m   3   increase in   PM 2.5    leads to about a 0.5 to 6\xa0percent drop in productivity \nand labor cost saving. Our findings suggest that \nreliable  real-time monitoring of policy outcomes at the local level could contribute \nto closing the enforcement gap as long as local officials face performance incen-\ntives. However, the existence of such performance incentives could at the same time \ndistort the behavior of local officials toward data manipulation. Therefore, the infor -\nmation provision system would need to be carefully designed to ensure accurate \n top-down accountability—e.g., by ensuring that information provision and enforce-\nment responsibilities are sufficiently separated.\nREFERENCES\nAcemoglu, Daron, Leopoldo Fergusson, James Robinson, Dario Romero, and Juan F. 213Informed Enforcement: Lessons  
from Pollution Monitoring in China†
By Sebastian Axbard and Zichen Deng*
Government regulations are often imperfectly enforced by pub-
lic officials. In this study, we exploit the introduction of air pollu-
tion monitors in China to investigate whether  real-time monitoring 
of policy outcomes affects the enforcement of existing regulations. 
Using assignment criteria established by the central government 
and new  georeferenced data on local enforcement activities, we 
show that monitoring (i) increases enforcement against local firms, 
(ii) improves the targeting of enforcement, and (iii) reduces aggre-
gate pollution. These effects are driven by officials facing perfor -
mance incentives and are stronger when there is limited scope for 
data manipulation, suggesting that  real-time monitoring improves 
 top-down accountability. (JEL   K32, L51, O13, P25, P28, Q52, Q53)
Across the globe, there is a substantial discrepancy between central government 
regulations and actual enforcement of those regulations at the local level. This 
gap exists across a wide range of policy areas and is particularly severe in low- and 
 middle-income countries (Nakagaki, Kompanek, and Tominic 2012; World Bank 
2017). A common practice to address the principal–agent problem inherent in the 
delegation of authority to lower levels of government is to provide  high-powered 
incentives to implementing officials to ensure that their interests are better aligned 
with those of the policymaker.1 However, such incentive schemes require reliable 
information on the actions of agents or local policy outcomes. In many settings, 
such information either is not widely available, is of poor quality, or could easily be 
manipulated by local officials who have an interest in misreporting due to the incen-
tives they face (Jacob and Levitt 2003; Figlio and Winicki 2005; Figlio and Getzler 
2006; Banerjee, Duflo, and Glennerster 2008; Sandefur and Glassman 2015; Fisman 
and Wang 2017; Greenstone et al. 2022; Acemoglu et al. 2020).
1 The theoretical literature has focused on how incentives could be designed to ensure the motivation of agents 
while decreasing any distortionary impact on effort (Holmström 1979; Holmström and  Milgrom 1991; Baker, 
Gibbons, and Murphy 1994).* Axbard: School of Economics and Finance, Queen Mary, University of London (email: s.axbard@qmul.
ac.uk); Deng: School of Economics, University of Amsterdam; Department of Economics, Norwegian School of 
Economics (email: z.deng@uva.nl). Benjamin Olken was coeditor for this article. We are grateful to seminar partic-
ipants at University of Bergen, University of Zurich, University of York, BI Norwegian Business School, University 
of Helsinki, CEIBS, NHH, University of Amsterdam, Renmin University, VU Amsterdam, Queen Mary University

disclosure statement(s) or to comment in the online discussion forum.214 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024
This paper explores how a technology that enables the central government to directly 
monitor local policy outcomes in real time can overcome the gap in enforcement. 
More specifically, we study the introduction of air pollution monitors in China—a set-
ting where local officials face strong incentives to reduce pollution under centrally set 
targets—and investigate how that affects local governments’ enforcement of air pol-
lution regulations as well as local pollution levels. Our focus on environmental policy 
is motivated by recent reporting from the United Nation ( 2019)  arguing that a lack of 
enforcement of environmental regulations is one of the greatest obstacles that needs 
to be overcome in order to combat climate change and pollution. Despite international 
efforts in recent years to improve air quality, more than 90 percent of the world’s pop-
ulation in 2016 ( WHO 2016)  still lived in areas where air pollution exceeded World 
Health Organization guidelines, with  far-reaching consequences for both health and 
productivity (Neidell and Currie 2005; Greenstone and Hanna 2014; Ebenstein et al. 
2017; Jia 2017; Barwick et al. 2018) . A large part of this population lived in emerging 
economies, including China, where pollution levels have exceeded the highest levels 
recorded in high-income countries.
We begin by investigating how a central-government-led program that introduced 
552 pollution monitors in 2015 has shaped the enforcement activities of city gov-
ernments in China. To conduct this analysis, we collect more than 55,000 environ-
mental enforcement records from local governments. We then classify these records 
and identify the firm involved, the type of regulation violated, and the punishment 
imposed. Using this information, we estimate a flexible  difference-in-difference 
(DiD)  model, which compares firms located close to a monitor with firms located 
farther away from the monitor but within the same city. The results show an increase 
in the probability of enforcement by 72 percent for firms located within 10 kilometers 
(km) of a monitor, consistent with anecdotal evidence suggesting that cities stepped 
up enforcement activities close to the monitors after their introduction (see discussion 
in Section IIIB) . The main threat to identification —potential endogenous placement 
of monitors—is mitigated in this setting because the placement of monitors followed 
strict guidelines issued by the central government. We investigate the determinants of 
monitor location and document that the placement is unrelated to prior enforcement 
activity and that there are no differential  pre-trends for firms located at different dis-
tances from the monitor. In addition, we show that air pollution monitoring does not 
affect enforcement related to other types of environmental regulations.
To shed further light on how government actions are affected, we investigate how 
the type of enforcement carried out changes in the presence of monitoring. We show 
that local governments impose stricter punishment against  high-polluting firms and 
become more responsive to local pollution shocks once monitors have been intro-
duced. To show the latter, we exploit exogenous variation in pollution induced by 
variations in rainfall and wind direction. We show that enforcement is higher when 
rainfall is low (and pollution is high) in the presence of monitoring, but that no such 
relationship exist when there is no monitoring. Similarly, the enforcement response 
is stronger against firms whose emissions will impact the monitor recording—i.e., 
firms that are located upwind from a monitor. This suggests that monitors can ensure 
a more responsive enforcement of regulations, mitigating concerns that our results 
are driven by a uniform increase in enforcement around all monitors.VOL. 16 NO. 1 215
AXBARD AND DENG: INFORMED ENFORCEMENT
Building on the above evidence that local enforcement efforts against firms increase 
in the vicinity of monitors, we move on to study the pollution monitoring program’s 
citywide effects. The focus on the  city level allows us to capture the aggregate impact 
of the policy ( including any within city spillover or displacement effect) .2 By exploit-
ing plausibly exogenous variation in the number of monitors installed in different 
cities, and thus the share of polluting activity covered by the program, we can assess 
the impact on total enforcement and pollution. To capture overall pollution changes 
at the  city level, we follow previous literature and use satellite data on the aerosol 
optical depth ( AOD). The AOD data enable us to measure pollution across the whole 
city both before and after the introduction of monitors and provide us with a reliable 
data source that cannot be manipulated by local officials. Our analysis exploits the 
fact that the central government assigned monitors to cities based on their population 
and geographical size. Using this information, we employ four different empirical 
strategies: a  DiD specification for cities that installed a different number of moni-
tors, an instrumental variable approach that uses the assigned number of monitors, 
a regression discontinuity ( RD) specification that exploits assignment cutoffs, and a 
 difference-in-discontinuity specification that combines the previous approaches. All 
four empirical strategies produce consistent estimates and show that one additional 
monitor, which increases coverage of  high-pollution activity by about 30 percent, 
leads to a  step-up in enforcement activities by between  15 and 28 percent and reduces 
pollution by 3. 1 to 4.6 percent. We then investigate spillovers and document that while 
enforcement activities are concentrated in the  high-pollution area close to the moni-
tors, pollution is reduced across the city.
Our preferred interpretation of the above results is that monitors improve the 
central government’s ability to hold local officials accountable for their actions. In 
this setting, local mayors face promotion incentives and are specifically evaluated 
on their ability to achieve predefined pollution reduction targets set by the central 
government. To empirically assess the validity of this interpretation, we follow Xi, 
Yao, and Zhang (2018) and exploit discontinuities in promotion incentives caused 
by the age of local mayors at the time of the National People’s Congress. Estimating 
our baseline empirical model for mayors facing different promotion probabilities, 
we find evidence suggesting that monitoring is the most effective when mayors face 
performance incentives. Hence, this finding is in line with pollution monitoring 
strengthening  top-down accountability and through that making existing perfor -
mance incentives more effective. Since  air pollution information is made available 
to the public online, an alternative mechanism explaining our results is that monitors 
improve  bottom-up accountability. However, additional analysis suggests that this is 
unlikely to be the main driver behind our results.3
2 As depicted in panel B of online Appendix Figure D2, cities are large geographical units. Due to the adminis-
trative structure in China and the large distance between the urban centers of different cities, we are not concerned 
about across city spillovers.
3 As discussed in Section IV , we do not suggest that the monitors did not improve access to information about 
local pollution to the public (which in turn may have an impact on government enforcement). However, the response 
in enforcement and pollution to more comprehensive monitoring that we document at the city level does not seem 
to be driven by increased dissemination of information to the public.216 AMERICAN ECONOMIC JOURNAL: APPLIED ECONOMICS JANUARY 2024
Finally, as discussed above, two reasons why information about policy outcomes 
may be lacking or of poor quality in low- and  middle-income countries are capac-
ity constraints and misreporting. The policy we study is potentially reducing both 
of these factors at the same time. To shed some light on the relative importance of 
the two factors, we take advantage of an additional policy shift—the reassignment 
of control of the monitors from the local government to external third parties. This 
reassignment decouples the information provision responsibility from the enforce-
ment of regulation responsibility and was conducted after it was discovered that sev-
eral local governments tried to manipulate the data from the monitors. By exploiting 
information from the monitors as well as our  satellite-based measure of pollution, 
we show that the monitor recordings are more strongly correlated with the satellite 
data when they are under the control of a third party—consistent with a reduction 
in manipulation. Following this logic, we further document that when monitors are 
under the control of the independent third party, the effect of an additional monitor 
on enforcement and pollution is substantially larger. This provides suggestive evi-
dence that not only the capacity to collect information but also the way in which this 
information is provided is important for  top-down accountability.
This paper contributes to three strands of literature. First, it relates to a grow-
ing empirical literature studying policies aimed at reducing pollution in developing 
countries. Prior work has documented that regulatory changes can bring about pol-
lution reduction (Greenstone and Hanna 2014; Tanaka 2015; Ebenstein et al. 2017) 
and that the incentives faced by both local leaders (Kahn, Li, and Zhao 2015) and 
auditors matter for policy outcomes (Duflo et al. 2013). However, the literature also 
emphasizes that enforcement of environmental regulations is a major challenge 
(see, e.g., discussion in Greenstone and Hanna 2014) and that we know little about 
how to improve it in developing countries (Shimshack 2014). For example, simply 
increasing the rate of environmental inspections does not seem to have any sub-
stantial impact on compliance and environmental outcomes due to the importance 
of regulatory discretion (Duflo et  al. 2018). Our findings suggest that improved 
monitoring of local pollution —a policy that strengthens  top-down accountability 
without reducing regulatory discretion—could be an effective way of addressing the 
enforcement gap and reducing pollution. Hence, our work suggests that automatic 
pollution monitoring could be an effective policy instrument to address high levels 
of pollution in developing countries. We also relate to two concurrent studies that 
investigate other dimensions of the same pollution monitoring program (Greenstone 
et al. 2022; Barwick et al. 2020). Barwick et al. (2020) investigate the impact of 
sharing air pollution information with the public and show how that leads to avoid-
ance behavior, while Greenstone et al. (2022) study how the updating of monitors in 
large cities (as opposed to the introduction of new monitors in smaller cities that we 
study) improved air pollution data quality and reduced the scope for manipulating 
the data. An additional related concurrent paper is He, Wang, and Zhang (2020), 
which studies how water pollution monitoring affects firm performance and docu-
ments that firms immediately upstream of a water monitor have lower productivity 
than those immediately downstream. Finally, a literature focusing on the United 
States documents strategic responses to  air quality monitoring (Auffhammer, Bento, 
and Lowe 2009; Grainger and Schreiber 2019; Zou 2021). Our work complements VOL. 16 NO. 1 217
AXBARD AND DENG: INFORMED ENFORCEMENT
earlier studies by showing how air pollution monitoring affects the enforcement 
behavior of local governments and aggregate pollution levels within a fixed reg-
ulatory framework. We shed light on the consequences of monitoring for govern-
ment performance, exploring how the responsiveness and targeting of enforcement 
is affected. In addition, we investigate the long-term impact on an aggregate and 
objective measure of pollution (the AOD).4
Second, we contribute to an extensive literature showing that monitoring and the 
provision of information can improve accountability and government performance 
(Besley and  Burgess 2002; Olken 2007; Snyder and  Strömberg 2010; Reinikka 
and Svensson 2005, 2011; Kosack and Fung 2014; Avis, Ferraz, and Finan 2018). 
While the broader literature has considered the impact of media as well as of audits, 
we are most closely aligned with recent work showing how information technol-
ogy affects government performance and efficiency (Duflo, Hanna, and Ryan 2012; 
Muralidharan, Niehaus, and Sukhtankar 2016; Dhaliwal and Hanna 2017; Banerjee 
et al. 2020). Proponents of such technological innovations have argued that they 
could increase efficiency, reduce the scope for manipulation, and be implemented at 
a relatively low cost. Our study differs from most of the previous work by focusing 
on monitoring of the final policy outcome (pollution) rather than intermediate inputs 
in policy production—such as public official attendance (Duflo, Hanna, and Ryan 
2012; Dhaliwal and  Hanna 2017) or transfer of funds (Muralidharan, Niehaus, 
and Sukhtankar 2016; Banerjee et al. 2020). While the monitoring of final policy 
outcomes might not always be feasible, it could mitigate concerns about multitask-
ing (Holmström and Milgrom 1991) associated with intermediate monitoring. We 
show that policy outcome monitoring can indeed be effective in the context of pollu-
tion. In addition, we expand prior work by studying how enforcement of regulations 
as opposed to public service provision is affected by monitoring. Third, we relate to 
a literature investigating the potentially distorting effect of  high-powered incentives 
on data reporting (Banerjee, Duflo, and Glennerster 2008; Fisman and Wang 2017; 
Acemoglu et al. 2020), including manipulating pollution data (Andrews 2008; Chen 
et al. 2013; Ghanem and Zhang 2014; Oliva 2015). We contribute to this literature 
by studying how control over the information infrastructure (shifting from local 
governments to external firms) is correlated with the quality of information as well 
as government actions and actual policy outcomes. While we are cautious when 
interpreting the results from this analysis due to the strong assumptions required for 
causal inference, it has the benefit that we can observe both potentially manipulated 
data from monitors and satellite data independent of government influence (and 
therefore also policy impact).
The paper is structured as follows. Section  I describes the context as well as 
the implementation of the pollution monitoring program we investigate. Then the

I. Background and Policy Description
This section provides background information and describes the context in which 
the national monitoring program studied in this paper was introduced. In Section IA, 
we describe the environmental policies in place in China during this period and 
discuss the local leaders’ role in achieving them. After that, the infrastructure put in 
place to monitor these policies’ implementation is described in Section IB. Section IC 
discusses how the information presented in this section guides our analysis.
A. Environmental Policies in China
While the Chinese government’s priority during the past decades has largely been 
to stimulate economic growth, attention has lately shifted toward environmental pol-
icies (Zheng and Kahn 2017).5 Starting in 2013, the National Air Quality Action 
Plan was set up to improve air quality by the end of 2017. As a part of China’s 
successful “war on pollution” (Greenstone and Schwarz 2018), the plan laid out 
the general ambition for the whole country and set differentiated goals for each 
region. In January 2014, the Ministry of Environmental Protection (MEP) entered 
into “contracts” with all 31 provinces and set up a  three-year air quality plan to 
decrease the concentration of particulate matter (PM) in the whole country. In each 
“contract,” an air quality target for 2017 was set—resulting in different percentage 
reduction targets of   PM 2.5  / PM 10    for each province relative to the 2012 level.6
These centrally set targets are implemented by local government officials, who 
are incentivized to fulfill them through  performance-based promotions. Promotions 
are the key instrument used in China to ensure that local officials carry out pol-
icies in line with the goals set by the central government (see Zheng and  Kahn 
2013, 2017, for further discussion of this topic). For a long time, the central gov-
ernment focused on economic performance and emphasized economic growth as 
the key evaluation criteria for local officials’ promotion (Chen, Li, and Lu 2018). 
However, from the Twelfth  Five-Year Plan onward, the central government has used 
the fulfilment of environmental performance targets as a requirement for the promo-
tion of local  mayors (Zheng and Kahn 2013).
5 The concentration of air pollutants in China is among the world’s highest and is a problem with serious health 
consequences. Average   PM 2.5    (particulate matter with a diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less) concentrations in 
2013 were 91 micrograms per cubic meter ( μg/ m   3  ), which is nine times the amount the World Health Organization 
considers safe. Estimates by Greenstone and Schwarz (2018) suggest that if these levels of pollution are sustained, 
it will result in a 6.5 year decline in life expectancy for the average resident.
6 For the list of targets by province, see Table C3 in online Appendix C.VOL. 16 NO. 1 219
